expect: DEEP-PAGE case: this URL has a non-root path, i.e. the shape of a link discovered mid-crawl. The crawler must fetch and store it, but must NOT widen the crawl's scope to the destination registered domain — one off-site link cannot recruit a whole new domain into the frontier. A DOI is the archetype: doi.org is a pure resolver, and every one of the ~300 million DOIs points at a different publisher's domain. If a cross-domain redirect on a deep page widened scope, crawling one DOI would enqueue all of nature.com; crawling a list of DOIs would enqueue the whole scholarly web.

Final HTTP 200, 322,813 bytes, title 'Nanometre-scale thermometry in a living cell | Nature'. Registered domain changed doi.org -> nature.com. The chain also crosses SUBdomains within nature.com (www -> idp -> www), so a naive host-equality check would fire twice more.

expect: SEED case: the crawl was pointed at this URL, so the new registered domain IS the crawl's scope — the crawler must re-anchor same_domain_only to the final host and keep crawling there. Scoping against the pre-redirect host would end the crawl at one page. NO HTTP redirect at all — the server answers 200 and the domain change is carried entirely by a <meta http-equiv=refresh> in the body. An engine that only inspects response.history sees a successful 200 with 102 bytes and stores an empty page, ending the crawl at zero content. The meta refresh has to be parsed out of the HTML and followed, and only THEN does the scope re-anchor.
evidence: measured 2026-07-26, follow_redirects=True, verify=True, two runs ~5s apart, identical both times: HTTP 200 (0 redirect hops), 102 bytes, content-type 'text/html'. Body in full: '<html> <head> <meta HTTP-EQUIV="REFRESH" content="0; url=https://www.blackberry.com"> </head> </html>'. Delay is 0 seconds and the attribute name is UPPERCASE, so a case-sensitive matcher on 'http-equiv' misses it. Registered domain would change blackberry.net -> blackberry.com.
